name: storytelling_007
user_goal:
Using this uploaded character portrait of the storyteller grandmother, produce an English-Spanish bilingual illustrated audiobook of this folk tale. The story to narrate, in full:

The Lion and the Mouse.

A lion was sleeping in his cave deep in the forest when a tiny mouse, scurrying across the floor, ran right over the lion's nose. The lion woke with a roar and pinned the mouse down with one great paw.

'Please, mighty lion, spare my life!' cried the little mouse. 'If you let me go, I promise I will repay your kindness someday.'

The lion laughed loudly. 'How could a tiny creature like you ever help a great lion like me?' But amused by the small thing's bravery, he lifted his paw and let the mouse scurry away.

Not many days later, the lion was hunting in the forest when he became tangled in a hunter's net. He roared and struggled, but the more he fought, the tighter the ropes wound around his huge body. The forest filled with his furious bellows.

The little mouse, hearing the lion's cries, came running. He found the great beast caught fast, helpless and angry. Without a word, the mouse began to gnaw on the heavy ropes with his sharp little teeth. He gnawed and gnawed, all through the long afternoon, until at last one strand parted, then another, and the lion was free.

'You laughed at me when I said I would help you someday,' said the mouse, looking up with bright eyes. 'Now you see — even the smallest friend can help the strongest, when help is needed most.'

And from that day on, the lion and the mouse were the closest of companions, and the lion never again mocked any creature for being small.

name: storytelling_012
user_goal: Here's my story I want to process: Beneath the crooked stone arch of an old city alleyway, a young violinist named Jude played every afternoon for whatever coins passersby would drop. He was not a famous musician. He had only a borrowed violin with a nick on its scroll, and a folding chair, and an open case at his feet. But he played with the seriousness of someone who believed music could make the city a better place. Most days, almost no one stopped. They walked past with their coffee and their phones, and at the end of each day Jude counted out enough coins for a sandwich and rode the last bus home to a tiny apartment he shared with his grandmother. He told himself he was not yet discouraged. But he was almost. On a rainy Tuesday, a thin gray cat wandered into the alley. She was small, with a torn ear and yellow eyes, and she sat down on the cobblestones three feet from Jude's chair and watched him play. When he stopped, she did not move. When he started again, she stayed. When he packed up for the day, she followed him as far as the alley's mouth and stopped. Jude watched her disappear into the rain. The next day she came back. She sat in the same spot. Jude began to call her Sonata, because she arrived so punctually with the beginning of his first piece. He began to bring her a bit of his sandwich. Sonata grew less thin. But something else began to happen. The cat seemed to hear the music as most people did not. When Jude played slowly, her eyes half-closed. When he played a quick passage, her tail flicked with the rhythm. Some days she even followed the music with a low, almost-purred hum. Passersby, noticing the strange devoted listener, began to stop too. A child pointed and laughed. A tired woman paused, then sat on the alley steps, then stayed for three whole pieces. A man with a briefcase dropped his first coin, then returned the next week and dropped another. Within a month, a small crowd gathered under the arch most afternoons. Sonata always took her place first. A violinist, the locals learned, was playing in the alley near the bakery, and he had an astonishing feline regular. Jude's coin case grew heavier. A music teacher stopped one Friday and gave him her card. A wedding planner wanted him for a small spring ceremony. Jude called his grandmother on his way home and she laughed at him for being starry-eyed, and then she cried a little, and then they had a better dinner than usual. On the day of his first paid wedding, Jude brought Sonata a whole tin of tuna and set it in the alley. He played one last song for her before the taxi came to take him uptown. Sonata ate the tuna and watched him go with her yellow eyes. She stayed in the alley. She became, in time, everyone's cat, fed by the bakery and the old shoe-repair shop. But every afternoon she still came to the arch at the hour Jude used to play, and she listened for a music only she remembered. — Make this into an illustrated audiobook with a gentle solo violin BGM — rainy-alley watercolor style

name: storytelling_015
user_goal:
Create an English-Chinese bilingual illustrated audiobook of this Hans Christian Andersen fairytale with a gentle harp-and-celesta BGM. Narrate in English; burn both English and Chinese subtitles. The story to narrate, in full:

It was terribly cold. Snow was falling, and it was almost dark, on the last evening of the old year, New Year's Eve. In the cold and the gloom, a poor little girl walked through the streets, bareheaded and barefoot. She had been wearing slippers when she left home, but they were not much use — they had belonged to her mother, and were so large the little one had lost them in running across the street to dodge two rushing carriages. One slipper was nowhere to be found; the other a boy snatched up and ran off with, saying he could use it as a cradle when he had children of his own.

So the little girl walked on, with her tiny naked feet blue with cold. In an old apron she carried a bundle of matches, and held one bunch in her hand. The whole day no one had bought any from her; no one had given her so much as a penny. Hungry and shivering, she crept along — a picture of misery, poor little thing.

Snowflakes settled on her long fair hair, which curled in pretty ringlets over her shoulders, but she paid no heed. Lights shone from every window; the savory smell of roast goose drifted out, for it was New Year's Eve. At last she crept into a corner between two houses, drew her little feet up under her, but felt colder still. She dared not go home — she had sold no matches, and would surely be beaten; besides, it was nearly as cold there, the wind howling through their roof though they had stuffed the largest cracks with rags and straw.

Her little hands were almost numb. Ah — a single match might do some good, if she dared draw one from the bundle, strike it on the wall, and warm her fingers! She drew one out — scratch! — how it spluttered and burned! It gave a warm bright flame, like a candle, when she held her hand around it. It seemed to the little girl that she sat in front of a great iron stove with polished brass feet and ornaments, the fire blazing blissfully. She stretched out her feet to warm them too — and the flame went out, the stove vanished, and only the charred match-end was left in her hand.

She struck another. It blazed up, and where the light fell on the wall the wall became transparent like gauze. She saw into a room where a snow-white tablecloth was spread, with fine china and a roast goose stuffed with apples and prunes, steaming gloriously. And — what was more wonderful still — the goose hopped down from the dish and waddled across the floor, knife and fork still in its breast, straight toward the little girl. Then the match went out, and only the cold thick wall remained.

She lit another. Now she sat under the most beautiful Christmas tree, larger and finer than the one she had peeped at through the rich merchant's glass doors. Thousands of candles burned on its green branches, and bright pictures, like those in shop windows, looked down upon her. The little girl reached out her hand — and the match went out. The Christmas lights rose higher and higher, until they were the twinkling stars of the sky. One fell, drawing a long line of fire.

'Someone is dying,' said the little girl. Her old grandmother — the only person who had ever been kind to her, and who was now dead — had told her: when a star falls, a soul is going up to God.

She struck another match against the wall. In its glow her grandmother stood before her, clear and shining, gentle and loving. 'Grandmother!' cried the child. 'Oh, take me with you! I know you will go away when the match goes out — vanish like the warm stove, the lovely roast goose, and the splendid Christmas tree!' And she hurriedly struck all the rest of the matches in the bundle, for she wanted to keep her grandmother near. The matches blazed with a brightness greater than the noonday sun. Grandmother had never looked so beautiful or so tall. She took the little girl in her arms, and they flew upward in joy and brightness, far above the earth — to where there was no cold, no hunger, no fear; they were with God.

In the cold morning hour, the little girl was found in the corner between the two houses, her cheeks rosy and a smile on her lips. Frozen to death on the last evening of the old year. The new year's sun rose on her stiff little body, with the matches, of which one bundle was nearly burned. 'She tried to warm herself,' people said. No one knew the beautiful things she had seen, nor in what glory she had gone with her grandmother into the joy of a new year.
